coredata.dc:description: Polyamide 4 (PA4) is a biobased plastic that has superior mechanical properties. PA4 shows good biodegradability in terrestrial and marine environments; however, the detailed interaction between PA4 and PA4-degrading enzymes from PA4-degrading microorganisms remains unclear. In this study, we isolated 11 novel strains of a PA4-degrading bacterium belonging to Pseudoalteromonas from a marine environment. Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5, which showed the highest PA4-degrading activity among the isolates, produced maximum PA4-degrading activity in culture supernatant after 4 days of incubation at 15 °C in Marine Broth 2216 containing 0.5 w/v% PA4 powder. We purified an enzyme that hydrolyzes PA4 at amide bonds into γ-aminobutyric acid oligomers (2–3 mers) from the culture supernatant. Based on a homology search using the amino acid sequence and predicted 3D structure of the enzyme, it was predicted to be composed of a substrate binding domain (SBD), linker domain, and catalytic domain (CD). The enzyme is a homodimer consisting of 75-kDa subunits, and the SBD is digested by autolysis in the absence of Ca2+. Interestingly, enzymatic properties, such as optimum temperature, pH, and NaCl concentration for high activity, differed between the full-size enzyme and autolyzed enzyme. In the predicted 3D structure of the enzyme, the structure of the CD overlapped with that of 6-aminohexanoate-dimer hydrolase, with a root mean square deviation of 1.084 Å. To our knowledge, this is the first report on the enzymatic and structural properties of a marine PA4-degrading enzyme. Our findings contribute to the understanding of the mechanisms of PA4 degradation in the marine environment.

ce:section.ce:para: A wide variety of plastic products are being used these days and unfortunately, most plastic products are discarded into the environment after use. It is estimated that 4.8–12.7 million tons of plastic waste are released into the marine environment each year [1,2]. Plastic wastes are not readily degraded in the environment and cause serious problems. For example, the amount of ghost fishing gear, such as fishing nets and ropes, has increased, affecting approximately 700 marine species [3]. In addition, microplastics, which are fragments of plastics that have been fragmented by physical or other actions, can be carriers of pathogenic microorganisms and harmful chemicals [4]. These microplastics are taken up by fish and shellfish and negatively affect not only marine life but also human health [5]. Therefore, measures are needed to solve the marine plastic pollution.

In recent years, biodegradable plastics have attracted attention as a solution to the marine plastic pollution. Biodegradable plastics, such as poly(lactic acid), poly(butylene succinate), polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA), and polycaprolactone (PCL), have been developed and are produced at an amount of 1.17 million tons per year [6]. It has been well investigated how these plastics are biodegraded in various environments; however, only PHA and PCL show biodegradability in both terrestrial and marine environments [7–9]. Therefore, new biobased plastics that are biodegradable in the marine environment are required.

Polyamide 4 (PA4), which is a biobased polyamide with a high melting point and superior mechanical strength, is expected to replace widely used petroleum-based plastics, such as polyamide 6 (PA6). PA4 can be synthesized by ring-opening polymerization of 2-pyrrolidone (2PRN), which is a cyclic form of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) [10]. GABA is produced by α-decarboxylation of glutamic acid by glutamic acid decarboxylase [11,12], and GABA production by microbial fermentation of biomass has been actively studied [13]. Zhang et al. performed a one-pot conversion of glutamate to 2PRN by expressing 2PRN synthase from Streptomyces aizunensis and glutamate decarboxylase in recombinant Escherichia coli [14], which indicates that the raw material of PA4 (2PRN) can be synthesized from biomass by a completely biotechnological process.

PA4 reportedly degrades in various environments, including the marine environment [15–20], whereas most polyamides, such as PA6 and PA6.6, are not readily degraded in natural environments [21–24]. The biodegradability of PA4 has been actively studied in active sludge [16], soils [17,18], river water, and seawater [19,20], and PA4-degrading microorganisms have been isolated [16,18,20,25]. Fungal isolates include Fusarium spp. from the soil [18] and bacterial isolates include Stenotrophomonas sp. from the soil [18] and Pseudomonas sp. from active sludge [16]. Recently, we for the first time successfully purified an extracellular PA4-degrading enzyme from soil-derived Pseudoxanthomonas sp. TN-N1 and reported its properties [25]. The enzyme hydrolyzes PA4 at amide bonds into GABA oligomers (2–4 mers). We suggested that Pseudoxanthomonas sp. TN-N1 would assimilate GABA and GABA oligomers produced from PA4 by the identified enzyme and other enzymes that convert GABA oligomers into GABA. There are few reports of PA4 biodegradation studies in marine environments [19,20]. Although PA4 biodegrades at the same rate as PCL in seawater [20], strain MND-1, which belongs to the family Alteromonadacea, is the only marine-derived PA4-degrading microorganism identified to date [25]. When the MND-1 strain was cultured in PA4-containing medium, GABA and GABA oligomers were detected in the culture supernatant, which suggests the presence of extracellular PA4-degrading enzymes in the marine environment. However, to date, PA4-degrading enzymes have not been identified from PA4-degrading microorganisms isolated from the marine environment.

In this study, we isolated novel PA4-degrading microorganisms from the marine environment and purified their PA4-degrading enzymes. In addition, we characterized a purified enzyme and predicted its 3D structure based on its amino acid sequence.

2-Pyrrolidone (Tokyo Chemical Industry UK Ltd., Tokyo, Japan), isophthaloyl dichloride (Tokyo Chemical Industry), and sodium (Kanto Chemical Co., Inc., Tokyo, Japan) were used for PA4 synthesis. Plysurf A210G, which was used to prepare PA4 emulsion as a surfactant, was purchased from DKS Co., Ltd. (Kyoto, Japan).

PA4 was synthesized as previously reported [26]. Ring-opening polymerization of 2PRN was carried out using isophthaloyl dichloride and sodium as the initiator and catalyst, respectively. The molecular mass of the polymerized PA4 was estimated to be Mn = 12,000, with Mw /Mn = 1.4, using analytical gel permeation chromatography [25].

Two PA4 films (3.5 × 4 cm) were attached to a plastic container and submerged at a depth of 15 or 43 m in Yamada Bay (N 39°28, E 141°59) from February to April 2021. The film surfaces were aseptically washed with artificial seawater. The wash water was spread on Marine Agar 2216 (Difco BD, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) plates containing 0.5 w/v% PA4 powder (PA4 plate medium) that were incubated at 15 °C for approximately 1 week to isolate the microorganisms attached to the PA4 films. Strains that formed clear zones on the agar plates were selected as PA4-degrading bacteria.

The isolated strains were cultured in Marine Broth 2216 (Difco BD) at 15 °C (160 strokes/m) for 24 h. Then, the cultures (3 mL) were inoculated into 500 mL culture flasks containing 150 mL of Marine Broth 2216 containing 0.5 w/v% PA4 (PA4 medium) and incubated at 15 °C with shaking (125 strokes/min) for an appropriate period. After incubation, the cultures were centrifuged at 7,670 × g at 4 °C for 10 min. The culture supernatants were subjected to enzyme activity assays as described in Section 2.7.

The isolated PA4-degrading strains were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing. Total genomic DNA was extracted using a NucleoSpin Microbial DNA kit (Macherey-Nagel, Duren, Germany) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The 16S rDNA gene fragment was amplified using KOD-Plus and primers 27f (5′-AGAGTTTGATCCTGGCTCAG-3′) and 1525r (5′-AAAGGAGGTGATCCAGCC-3′) in a 50 μL reaction volume. The thermal cycling program was as follows: 94 °C for 3 min followed by 30 cycles of 98 °C for 10 s and 68 °C for 90 s. The PCR products were purified using NucleoSpin Gel and PCR Clean-up (Macherey-Nagel), and sequenced at Eurofins Genomics K.K. (Tokyo, Japan). The 16S rRNA sequences were analyzed using nucleotide BLAST [27].

The phenotypic characteristics of strain No. 5, which showed the highest PA4-degrading activity among all isolated strains, were determined according to a previously described method [28,29]. Growth at different temperatures and NaCl concentrations was determined by measuring the absorbance at 660 nm after 24 h of incubation in medium B (0.2 w/v% peptone, 0.2 w/v% casein hydrolysate, 0.2 w/v% yeast extract, 0.1 w/v% glucose, 0.002 w/v% KH2PO4, 0.005 w/v% MgSO4·7H2O, 50 v/v% artificial seawater, and 50 v/v% distilled water, pH 7.5–7.8) [28]. The utilization of various carbon sources was determined using BM broth [50 mM tris(hydroxymethyl)aminomethane, 190 mM NH4Cl, 0.33 mM K2HPO4·3H2O, 0.1 mM FeSO4·7H2O, 50 v/v% artificial seawater, and 50 v/v% distilled water, pH 7.5] [29].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Cultivation of the isolated strain and purification of the PA4-degrading enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: Strain No. 5 was cultured in Marine Broth 2216 at 15 °C (160 strokes/min). The culture (3 mL) was inoculated into a 500 mL culture flask containing 150 mL of PA4 medium and incubated at 15 °C with shaking (125 strokes/min) for an appropriate period. After incubation, the culture was centrifuged at 7,670 × g at 4 °C for 10 min.

The PA4-degrading enzyme was purified by ammonium sulfate precipitation. All procedures were performed at 5–10 °C. The culture supernatant was added to ammonium sulfate at a concentration of 40 w/v%. The enzyme solution was stirred for 1 h and the supernatant was collected by centrifugation at 9,900 × g at 4 °C for 20 min. Subsequently, ammonium sulfate was added to the supernatant to reach a final concentration of 50%. The enzyme solution was stirred for 3 h and centrifuged at 9,900 × g at 4 °C for 20 min. The precipitate was collected and dialyzed against artificial seawater for 24 h. ce:section.ce:section-title: Cloning of the PA4-degrading enzyme and prediction of its 3D structure
ce:section.ce:para: The purified enzyme was digested in-gel with trypsin, and the peptide fragments were analyzed using nano liquid chromatograph-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) (LTQ-Orbitrap XL; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The open reading frame (ORF) encoding the PA4-degrading enzyme in the draft genome of strain No. 5 was identified through a MASCOT search (http://www.matrixscience.com/home.html) of the peptide fragment sequences.

Genomic DNA was extracted from strain No. 5 using an Illustra bacteria genomicPrep Mini Spin Kit (Cytiva, Tokyo, Japan). The enzyme gene was amplified by PCR using primers pC-5_101-F (5′-AGGTAATACCATATGAAGAACAAATCGATACTCAT-3′) and pC-5_101-R (5′-AGCAGAGATTACCTATTAATTACACATACTACGAATTTTA-3′). The thermal cycles were as follows: 94 °C for 2 min followed by 30 cycles of 94 °C for 15 s and 55 °C for 30 s, and finally, 68 °C for 129 s. Similarly, the pColdⅣ vector (TaKaRa, Tokyo, Japan) was PCR-amplified using primers pColdⅣ-F (5′-TAGGTAATCTCTGCTTAAAAGC-3′) and pColdⅣ-R (5′-CATATGGTATACCTCTTATAAAT-3′). The thermal cycles were as follows: 94 °C for 2 min followed by 30 cycles of 94 °C for 15 s and 55 °C for 30 s, and finally, 68 °C for 4.3 min. The plasmid for enzyme expression, pColdⅣ-PA4 pa , was constructed by an infusion reaction of both PCR products using 5 × In-fusion HD Enzyme Premix at 37 and 80 °C for 15 min each.

The full amino acid sequence of the PA4-degrading enzyme was analyzed using protein BLAST [27]. The 3D structure of the enzyme was predicted using Alphafold2 (https://colab.research.google.com/github/sokrypton/ColabFold/blob/main/AlphaFold2.ipynb) based on the amino acid sequence without signal peptide. Proteins with similar structures were identified by feeding the predicted 3D structures to the Dali server (http://ekhidna2.biocenter.helsinki.fi/dali/). The 3D structure was analyzed using ChimeraX v.1.5 [30].

PA4-degrading activity was measured using PA4 emulsion prepared as described previously [16]. The reaction mixture contained 100 µL of culture supernatant or enzyme solution, 100 µL of the PA4 emulsion, and 100 µL of artificial seawater. As a control reaction, we used an enzyme solution that was denatured by heating at 100 °C for 10 min. The mixtures were incubated in 96-well plates at 15 °C with shaking. PA4-degrading activity was assessed by measuring the absorbance at 655 nm using a microplate reader (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA). One unit of PA4-degrading activity was defined as a decrease in absorbance at a rate of 655 nm per hour.

The effect of mineral salts in artificial seawater on enzyme autolysis was investigated. The purified enzyme was dialyzed in 30 mM HEPES buffer (pH 8.0) containing mineral salts (355 mM NaCl, 46.6 mM MgCl2, 24.7 mM Na2SO4, 9.02 mM CaCl2, 8.00 mM KCl, or 2.04 mM NaHCO3) at 4 °C for 24 h These mineral salt concentrations reflect those in artificial seawater. The dialyzed enzyme solution was assessed for PA4-degrading activity using the buffers used for dialysis. In addition, the enzyme was subjected to SDS-PAGE to determine its molecular weight.

The N-terminal amino acid sequence of the autolyzed enzyme was determined using Edman degradation [31]. The autolyzed enzyme was transferred from the SDS-PAGE gel to a Sequi-Blot PVDF Membrane (Bio-Rad Laboratories). The membrane was sent to Hokkaido System Science Co., Ltd. (Hokkaido, Japan) for determining the N-terminal five residues of the autolyzed enzyme.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of temperature, pH, and NaCl concentration on the PA4-degrading activities of intact and autolyzed enzymes
ce:section.ce:para: The autolyzed enzyme was prepared by dialyzing purified enzyme in 30 mM HEPES buffer (pH 8.0) for 24 h. The optimum temperature was measured in artificial seawater at various temperatures (5–65 °C). The optimum pH was measured in several buffers (pH 6.0–10.0) at 15 °C. For thermostability testing, the intact enzyme or autolyzed enzyme was incubated in artificial seawater at several temperatures (5–65 °C) for 2 h, and activity was measured in artificial seawater at 15 °C. For pH stability testing, the intact enzyme or autolyzed enzyme was incubated in several buffers (pH 6.0–10.0) at 15 °C for 2 h, and activity was measured in artificial seawater at 15 °C. The optimum NaCl concentration for the intact enzyme was measured in 30 mM HEPES buffer (pH 8.0) containing 18.04 mM CaCl2 and NaCl at various concentrations (0–1 M) at 15 °C. The intact enzyme was dialyzed for 24 h in the same buffer with various NaCl concentrations (0–1 M) for optimum NaCl concentration testing. The optimum NaCl concentration for the autolyzed enzyme was measured 30 mM HEPES buffer (pH 8.0) containing NaCl at various concentrations (0–1 M) at 15 °C. The autolyzed enzyme was dialyzed for 24 h in the same buffer with various NaCl concentrations (0–1 M) for optimum NaCl concentration testing.

PA4 emulsion was adjusted to an absorbance of 3.0 at a wavelength of 660 nm. The enzyme was prepared by dialyzing purified enzyme in 30 mM HEPES buffer (pH 8.0) containing 18.04 mM CaCl2. Two milliliters of a reaction mixture solution containing PA4 emulsion, enzyme (0.63 mg), and artificial seawater was incubated at 15 °C for 48 h. As a control reaction, we used an enzyme solution that was denatured by heating at 100 °C for 10 min. After the reaction, the reaction solutions were freeze-dried.

LC-MS analysis of the reaction products was performed as reported previously [25]. The reaction products were extracted from freeze-dried samples using acetonitrile. The reaction solution (1 μL) was analyzed using a single quadrupole LC-MS-2020 (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan). LC-MS was performed on a C18M 2D column (2 mm × 150 mm; Showa Denko) at 40 °C with a flow rate of 0.2 mL/min in gradient mode using acetonitrile and water as eluents. The acetonitrile concentration was set at 20% in the first min and then linearly increased to 50% over 9 min. Finally, the concentration was reduced to 20% and maintained for 5 min.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of culture conditions on PA4-degrading enzyme production by Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5
ce:section.ce:para: The isolated strain, Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5, was cultured in a 500 mL flask containing 150 mL of PA4 medium at 15 °C or 30 °C for 5 days, and PA4-degrading activity in the culture supernatant was measured daily (Fig. 2 ). When the strain was cultivated at 15 °C, bacterial growth and PA4-degrading activity increased over time until days 2 and 4, respectively. While growth was saturated after 2 days of cultivation, PA4-degrading activity decreased over time after 4 days of cultivation. On day 4, the PA4 powder in the medium was completely degraded. In contrast, under cultivation at 30 °C in PA4 medium, growth was good, but PA4-degrading activity was not detected in the culture supernatant. Therefore, we harvested culture supernatant after 3 or 4 days of cultivation at 15 °C to obtain the enzyme exhibiting PA4-degrading activity for further experiments. GABA monomers were detected in the culture supernatant by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analysis (Fig. S2), indicating that Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5 degrades PA4 into GABA monomers.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Identification of the PA4-degrading enzyme gene
ce:section.ce:para: The purified enzyme was digested in-gel with trypsin, and the peptide fragments were analyzed using nano LC-MS/MS. The ORF encoding the PA4-degrading enzyme in the draft genome of Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5 was identified from 3,744 ORFs using the peptide fragment sequences obtained by nano LC-MS/MS analysis. The supernatant fraction of a cell lysate of E. coli BL21 (DE3) harboring the identified ORF showed functional expression of the PA4-degrading enzyme as indicated by the results of a PA4-degrading activity assay and SDS-PAGE analysis (Table S1 and Fig. S4). Thus, we successfully cloned the PA4-degrading enzyme gene from Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5.

The ORF consists of 2,151 bp and encodes 716 amino acids (DDBJ Accession No. LC765678) (Fig. 4 ). The molecular mass was estimated to be 78,267 Da, which was almost consistent with the molecular mass of the subunits of the purified enzyme (75 kDa, Fig. 3). A 19-amino acid sequence in the N-terminal region (M1–A19) is typical of a sec‑dependent signal peptide [32]. A BLAST homology search using the full amino acid sequence revealed that the Y438–G568 region of the enzyme is homologous to AmpC β-lactamase [33]. The amino acid sequence in that region contains an amino acid motif (S-X-X-K) (S439-K442) conserved in the β-lactamase family, and S439 was presumed to be the catalytic center [33,34]. In fact, the PA4-degrading activity of the purified enzyme was inhibited by serine protease inhibitors (Table S2).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Prediction of the 3D structure of the enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: We predicted the 3D structure of the enzyme based on the amino acid sequence without signal peptide, using Alphafold2 (Fig. 5 A). In the 3D structure, the N-terminal region of the enzyme was composed of a β-sandwich structure, and the C-terminal region comprised a β-barrel structure and a typical β-lactamase structure (α and α/β domains). When the full range of predicted 3D structures was fed to the Dali server, the structure of the N-terminal region (Q20–G158) was predicted to be similar to that of the carbohydrate-binding module of some polysaccharide-degrading enzymes (PDB ID: 2XOM [35], 4QPW [36], and 1K42 [37]). The C-terminal region (G214–N716) structure was predicted to be similar to the structure of some β-lactamase family proteins (PDB ID: 7MDF [38], 6D3G [39], and 5NJ2 [40]) and that of a 6-aminohexanoate (Ahx)-dimer hydrolase S112A/G181D/H266N/D370Y mutant (NylB mutant) (PDB ID: 2ZMA) [41]. Based on these results, we predicted that the enzyme is composed of three domains: a substrate binding domain (SBD, Q20–G158), linker domain (LD, E159–S213) and catalytic domain (CD, G214–N716) (Figs. 4 and 5A). In ChimeraX, the C-terminal region (G214–N716) of the enzyme and NylB overlapped, with a root mean square deviation of 1.084 Å (Fig. 5B).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Autolysis of the purified enzyme from Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5 and effect of autolysis on enzymatic properties
ce:section.ce:para: Through experimenting, interestingly, we found that the purified enzyme was degraded to 61 kDa when it was incubated in HEPES buffer. We assumed that this was due to autolysis. To identify the main cause of autolysis, the purified enzyme was dialyzed against buffers containing one of six mineral salts found in artificial seawater. The molecular mass of the enzyme decreased in all buffers, except the one containing Ca2+ (Fig. 6 A). In addition, the PA4-degrading activity of the enzyme was strongly reduced in the presence of all mineral salts, except calcium ions (Fig. 6B). The N-terminal amino acid sequence of the autolyzed enzyme revealed that the enzyme was digested at G158–E159, between the SBD and LD (Figs. 4 and 5A). In addition, the molecular mass of the autolyzed enzyme prepared by dialyzing the purified enzyme in 30 mM HEPES buffer (pH 8.0) for 24 h was determined using a gel filtration column. The molecular mass of the autolyzed enzyme was estimated to be 117 kDa, indicating that the enzyme consists of a homodimer even after autolysis.

Next, we examined the effects of temperature, pH, and the NaCl concentration on PA4-degrading activity of the intact and autolyzed enzymes (Fig. 7 ). Maximum PA4-degrading activity of the intact enzyme was observed at 55 °C or pH 8.0 (Fig. 7A, C). In contrast, maximum activity of the autolyzed enzyme was observed at 35 °C or pH 9.5 (Fig. 7A, C), which differed from the optimum temperature and pH of the intact enzyme. However, there were no significant differences in stability at various temperatures and pH between the intact and autolyzed enzymes (Fig. 7B, D). The optimal NaCl concentration for PA4-degrading activity was 0 M for the intact enzyme and 0.7 M for the autolyzed enzyme (Fig. 7E). Next, we performed kinetic analysis of the intact and autolyzed enzymes (Fig. S5 and Table S3). Maximum degradation rates in artificial seawater were 0.124 mg/mL for the intact enzyme and 0.132 mg/mL for the autolyzed enzyme (Fig. S5). The K and ks values were 6.33 mL/mg and 2.33 U, respectively, for the intact enzyme, and 8.65 mL/mg and 0.278 U for the autolyzed enzyme (Table S3).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Reaction products of enzyme-mediated PA4 depolymerization
ce:section.ce:para: The reaction solution containing PA4 and the purified enzyme were analyzed by LC-MS. Peaks were identified in the chromatograms for both the reaction solution (Fig. 8 A) and the control solution (Fig. 8B). In the reaction solution (Fig. 8A), peaks were observed at 2.2 min and 2.8 min, and mass numbers (m/z) of 477, 274, 239, and 189 were strongly detected in positive mode. The peaks at m/z = 477 and 239 can be associated HEPES because these two peaks were also observed in the control solution (Fig. 8B). However, peaks at m/z = 274 and 189 were specifically observed in the reaction solution (Fig. 8A), indicating that these two peaks correspond to the main reaction products. NMR spectra of the reaction solution (Figs. S6 and S7) indicated that the peaks at m/z = 274 and 189 correspond to trimers and dimers of GABA, respectively. Therefore, we concluded that the enzyme hydrolyzes PA4 at amide bonds into GABA oligomers (2–3 mers).

We isolated 11 novel strains of a PA4-degrading bacterium from the marine environment. To date, only strain MND-1 belonging to the family Alteromonadaceae had been identified from the marine environment [20]. We may have found this novel PA4-degrading bacterium because we used a different cultivation temperature during screening from that used in the previous study. In the previous study, PA4-degrading microorganisms were screened on PA4 agar at 30 °C, whereas we carried out the screening using the same medium at 15 °C. In fact, the strains isolated in this study formed clear zones on PA4 agar only at 15 °C, and Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5 produced PA4-degrading enzyme at 15 °C, but not at 30 °C (Fig. 2). Therefore, we assume that some PA4-degrading microorganisms in the marine environment would be adapted to the low temperature of the habitat. Our findings indicate the importance of screening in conditions that mimic the natural environmental conditions of the isolates.

Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5 seems to degrade PA4 at a rate comparable to or faster than that of previously isolated PA4-degrading strains [16,18,20,25]. Our strain completely degraded PA4 powder in 4 days of incubation at 15 °C (Fig. 2). When Yamano et al. conducted a PA4 degradation assay of strain MND-1 using a biochemical oxygen demand test, the degradation rate was saturated at 50% after 5 days of incubation [20]. Pseudoxanthomonas sp. TN-N1, which is a PA4-degrading bacterium we previously isolated from soil, degraded 0.5 w/v% PA4 powder in 3 days of incubation at 30 °C, and Pseudomonas sp. ND-1 degraded 0.5 w/v% PA4 powder after 2 weeks of incubation at 25 °C.

Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5 secreted the enzyme during cultivation in PA4 medium at 15 °C, but no PA4-degrading activity was detected at 30 °C (Fig. 2). PA4-degrading activity was not detected when the strain was cultured at 15 °C in medium without PA4 (Fig. S8). These results indicated that PA4-degrading enzyme production is induced by temperature and the presence of PA4 and/or its degradation products. Pseudoxanthomonas sp. TN-N1 also produced PA4-degrading enzyme only in medium containing PA4 [25]. It is interesting to note that PA4 and PA4 degradation products, which are probably not present in nature, induce the secretion of the PA4-degrading enzyme. There may exist a natural substrate for the PA4-degrading enzyme that is structurally similar to PA4 or its degradation products. It is known that PCL, a petroleum-derived synthetic plastic that is biodegraded in the marine environment, is degraded by cutinase, and cutinase production is induced in PCL-degrading microorganisms by its degradation products [42–44]. This is presumably because of chemical structural similarity between the PCL degradation products of PCL and cutin monomers [42,45]. To find a potential natural substrate for the PA4-degrading enzyme, we focused on its characteristics. The identified PA4-degrading enzyme was predicted to have a β-lactamase structure containing Ser as an active center residue based on a homology search using the amino acid sequence and the predicted 3D structure. However, although PA4-degrading activity of the enzyme was inhibited by serine protease inhibitors, β-lactamase activity was not observed when nitrocefin, a typical β-lactamase substrate, was used as a substrate (data not shown). Further research is required to elucidate whether a natural substrate for the PA4-degrading enzyme that is structurally similar to the PA4 degradation products exists.

Based on a homology search and its predicted 3D structure, the PA4-degrading enzyme was predicted to be composed of an SBD, LD, and CD (Figs. 4 and 5A). Enzymes that degrade polymers, such as polysaccharide-degrading enzymes and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) depolymerase (PhaZ), are composed of the same domains [46,47]. These enzymes are known to adsorb to their substrate (i.e., the polymer surface) using the SBD and hydrolyze the substrate via the CD. The LD connects the SBD and CD. The predicted domains of the PA4-degrading enzyme are expected to have functions similar to those of polysaccharide-degrading enzymes and PhaZ.

We found that the PA4-degrading enzyme was autolyzed and the PA4-degrading activity of the enzyme was reduced in the absence of Ca2+ (Fig. 6). Autolysis has been reported for many proteases [48–51]. While some proteases mature and become catalytically active through autolysis [51], for others, autolysis leads to irreversible inactivation [50,52]. In general, autolysis of proteases is related to pH, temperature, or Ca2+ [48,49,52,53]. Some proteases (e.g., calpain) are estimated to autolyze by partial unfolding in the absence of Ca2+ [54]. For the PA4-degrading enzyme, as for calpain, Ca2+ appears to play a role in autolysis and enzyme activity. Likely, a lack of Ca2+ causes partial unfolding of the enzyme and subsequently, autolysis.

The autolysis site was located in the loop region of G139–T183 in the predicted 3D conformation of the PA4-degrading enzyme (Figs. 4 and 5A), and the autolyzed enzyme lost the SBD. Some enzymatic properties, such as the optimum temperature, pH, and NaCl concentration, and kinetic parameters differed between the intact and autolyzed enzymes (Fig. 7 and Table S3). In line herewith, PhaZ from a marine bacterium also showed altered enzymatic properties after loss of the SBD [55]. In accordance with the results for the PA4-degrading enzyme, the activity of PhaZ lacking the SBD also increased with increasing NaCl concentration because NaCl affected the hydrophobic interaction between the polymer surface and the enzyme. However, loss of the SBD in PhaZ did not affect the optimum temperature and pH. Regarding the kinetic parameters, loss of the SBD in PhaZ decreased the K value, but had no effect on the ks value. In contrast, for the PA4-degrading enzyme, loss of the SBD significantly increased the K value and decreased the ks value. These inconsistencies in the effect of loss of the SBD imply that the role of the SBD in the PA4-dgrading enzyme at least partially differs from that in PhaZ.

In the conformation predicted using AlphaFold2, the structure of the CD was similar to that of a NylB mutant (Fig. 5B). NylB is found in Arthrobacter sp. K172, which was isolated from the wastewater of a nylon plant, and can hydrolyze Ahx linear oligomers (2–6 mers) [56]. Negoro et al. identified the detailed catalytic mechanism and the residues involved in Ahx linear dimer degradation through X-ray crystallography of NylB [41,57–60]. Three amino acid residues (S439/K442/Y535) of the PA4-degrading enzyme spatially overlapped with the catalytic triad (S112/K115/Y215) of NylB (Fig. 5B). Therefore, we presumed that S439/K442/Y535 was the catalytic triad in the PA4-degrading enzyme (Fig. 5A, B). Furthermore, analysis of the reaction products suggested that like NylB, the PA4-degrading enzyme can hydrolyze the substrate at amide bonds (Fig. 8). Therefore, we expected the PA4-degrading enzyme, like NylB, to be able to degrade PA6 and Ahx oligomers. However, PA6 and Ahx linear dimer were not hydrolyzed by the purified PA4-degrading enzyme (data not shown). This is probably because of the shape of the catalytic cleft of the PA4-degrading enzyme. When NylB degrades Ahx oligomers, the loop region containing Y170 opens and closes, and Y170 forms a hydrogen bond with the nitrogen atom of the amide bond [59]. However, no structure corresponding to the loop region or Y170 of NylB was found in the PA4-degrading enzyme. Furthermore, in NylB, D181, Y370, and H375 are involved in the bonding with both ends of Ahx oligomers, but the residues corresponding to D181 and H375 are different in the PA4-degrading enzyme. Y370 of NylB is located in a similar position as in the PA4-degrading enzyme (Y377 of the PA4-degrading enzyme), but the orientation of the side chain is reversed. Therefore, it is likely that the PA4-degrading enzyme is unable to degrade Ahx oligomers because of structural differences other than in these three catalytic residues.

In LC-MS analysis of the reaction products, GABA trimers and dimers were mainly detected (Fig. 8), which suggests that this enzyme is an endo-type enzyme that hydrolyzes PA4 at amide bonds to produce GABA oligomers. This result is in line with our previous report of PA4 degradation by Pseudoxanthomonas sp. TN-N1 [25]. Notably, GABA dimers were the main degradation product, as the intensity of the peak at m/z = 189 (dimer) was substantially higher than that of the peak at m/z = 274 (trimer), and m/z = 359 (tetramer) was not observed (Fig. 8). This indicates that the PA4-degrading enzyme derived from Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5 can degrade PA4 into lower-molecular-weight products than that derived from Pseudoxanthomonas sp. TN-N1. However, although GABA monomers were detected in the culture supernatant (Fig. S2), they were not detected in the reaction solution containing PA4 and the purified enzyme using LC-MS and 1H NMR. This suggests that Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5 would produce the identified enzyme and other enzymes that convert GABA oligomers into GABA. Further research is required to elucidate this mechanism.

We isolated 11 novel strains of a PA4-degrading bacterium from the marine environment and successfully purified the enzyme that depolymerizes PA4 into GABA oligomers from Pseudoalteromonas sp. Y-5. We predicted the 3D structure of the purified enzyme and identified the catalytic triad (S439/K442/Y535). The enzyme was predicted to consist of an SBD, LD, and CD. The enzyme autolyzed in the absence of Ca2+, which altered the optimal conditions for PA4 degradation and provided information on the role of the SBD. To our knowledge, this is the first report on the enzymatic and structural properties of a PA4-degrading enzyme isolated from a marine bacterium. Our results are expected to contribute to furthering our understanding of microbial degradation of PA4, a non-natural compound, and to the development of biodegradable plastics and enzymatic recycling technologies for plastics in the marine environment.
